title: An iPad for Video Calls With Mom or Dad: Big Text, Simple Setup and How to Lock It Down
subtitle: How the Apple iPad and iPad mini compare for video calls, and the built-in settings that can help a parent use one, with a few cautions.
excerpt: A tablet can turn a phone call into a face-to-face visit. Here is what the iPad and iPad mini cost, what they cannot do, and how to set one up with fewer distractions for a parent.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: A phone call is nice, but seeing a grandchild's face is better. For many older adults, though, a smartphone screen is small, the buttons are fiddly, and every app seems to want an update or a password. A tablet gives you a bigger picture, larger text and room to tap without hitting the wrong thing.

The catch is that a tablet like the iPad is a full computer. Out of the box it can feel just as busy as a phone. Apple builds in settings that a family member can use to simplify it. This guide covers which iPad to consider, what it costs, and how to set it up for a parent.
How video calls on an iPad work

Apple's own app for video calls is FaceTime. It is simple, but it has one big limit: FaceTime only connects Apple devices. If a son, daughter or grandchild uses an Android phone, they cannot join a FaceTime call from the iPad. Before you buy, check what phones the family uses and which video app everyone already has.

The iPad also needs an internet connection for calls. The standard Wi-Fi model works only where there is Wi-Fi, such as a home network. The Wi-Fi + Cellular model, Apple says, "lets you connect when Wi-Fi isn't available." It costs $150 more on both models, and cellular also needs a data plan from a carrier. Apple's pages mention carrier deals and financing but do not explain those fees or say what a plan costs, so ask the carrier directly.

The review site Caring Village says Apple supports each iPad generation with software for a long time. That is worth knowing if you want a tablet that stays supported for years, though it is not a promise about any one device.

items: Wi-Fi or cellular: if your parent has home Wi-Fi, the Wi-Fi model is usually enough and avoids a monthly data bill.
Storage: both models start at 128GB, with 256GB and 512GB also offered. Higher sizes cost more.
Screen size: Caring Village lists the standard iPad as 11-inch; Apple's page does not state it. Check the size on Apple's page for the model you buy, and compare the two in a store if you can.

Built-in accessibility: Caring Village lists text size, VoiceOver, Magnifier and AssistiveTouch among the iPad's built-in accessibility features. Look in Settings, then Accessibility, to see what each one does.
Trade-in: Apple's pages mention savings with trade-in, up to $915. The amount depends on the device you trade in and is not a guaranteed value. The mini's offer applies to an iPad 6 or newer.
Setup help: plan on a family member doing the first setup in person. An iPad is not a one-button device.
Prices change: the prices below were on Apple's pages in November 2026 and may have moved, so check current price before you buy.

sections.content: Setting it up for a parent

Start with the basics in Settings. The Accessibility section is where Apple keeps options such as larger text, and it is worth exploring together. Taking off apps your parent does not need can also reduce clutter. For many older adults, that may be enough.

Apple also offers a mode called Assistive Access. Apple describes it as a feature that "makes it easier for people with cognitive disabilities to use iPad independently." It simplifies apps and layout, and the included apps are Calls, Camera, Messages, Music, Photos and Magnifier, among others. Because it is designed for cognitive disabilities, it may be more than an older adult needs. If memory or thinking concerns are the reason you are considering it, check with your parent's doctor first.

You find it in Settings, then Accessibility, then Assistive Access. Apple's setup guide says a "trusted supporter," such as a family member or caregiver, can help choose the apps. You set an Assistive Access passcode, and the person using it needs to know the device passcode.

An iPad is not a safety device. It does not detect falls and cannot call for help on its own. If your parent needs that, look at a medical alert system. Simplified settings can cut down on clutter but do not stop every scam text or pop-up, so talk with your parent about never sharing passwords or payment details. In an emergency, call 911.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: If your parent will use the iPad in bed or at the kitchen table, a stand makes calls more comfortable; see our separate guide to tablet stands.
Choosing a tablet for someone you love is really about the calls that come after. Set it up together, keep it simple, and do a practice call or two before you leave.

products.name: Apple iPad (11-inch, A16), Wi-Fi
products.price: From $449 for 128GB Wi-Fi; 128GB Wi-Fi + Cellular from $599 (Apple list price, November 27, 2026). Check current price.
products.blurb: Suits families who want a larger screen (Caring Village lists it as 11-inch) at a lower price than the mini. Comes in blue, silver, pink and yellow, with a cellular option for use away from Wi-Fi.

products.name: Apple iPad mini, Wi-Fi
products.price: From $699 for 128GB Wi-Fi; 128GB Wi-Fi + Cellular from $849 (Apple list price, November 27, 2026); nano-texture glass options cost more. Check current price.
products.blurb: Suits someone who prefers the mini size and wants Apple's A20 Pro chip. It costs more than the standard iPad, so compare the two for size and price before you choose.
